newsitem.title: USA: N.Carolina trial opens in racially-linked murders.
newsitem.headline: N.Carolina trial opens in racially-linked murders.

text.p: A former soldier at Fort Bragg went on trial Tuesday for the 1995 murder of two black residents in what police said was a racially-motivated crime.

Jury selection began in the civilian trial of James Burmeister, 22, a former private in the elite 82nd Airborne Division at Fort Bragg, who is charged with the Dec. 8, 1995, slayings of Jackie Burden and Michael James in Fayetteville.
Burmeister's co-defendant, Malcolm Wright, is scheduled to go on trial separately in March.

A third soldier, Randy Meadows, was charged with driving Burmeister and Wright to the area where the killings took place. Last week Meadows, 22, pleaded guilty to assault charges and agreed to testify for the prosecution.

Prosecutors are expected to call as witnesses acquaintances of the three men, who were described as members of a white supremacist group. Police found skinhead literature, a Nazi flag and a book on how to make a bomb in a trailer Burmeister rented at the time of his arrest.
Court records and police reports alleged that the soldiers left a bar to search for blacks or drug dealers to attack on the night of the crime, and spotted James and Burden walking on a street.
James was shot in the head and Burden died from bullet wounds to her head and back.
Police said Meadows told them that Burmeister wanted to earn a "spider web tattoo," a symbol that police say indicates the wearer has killed a homosexual or black.
Following the shootings, Army Secretary Togo West ordered an examination of racism and extremism in Army ranks. Investigators concluded there was little evidence of racism in the U.S. military.
The three men were dishonourably discharged by the military after their arrests and were charged with the murders in a civilian court.
Prosecutors said they would seek the death penalty in the trial before Superior Court Judge Coy Brewer.
